title: Part 4
text: ozone hit at once, sharp enough to make the eyes water. He shifted the angle of the blade, wedged it deeper into the widening gap, and pried. Bits of metal snapped and jumped away from the edge, the band positively shrieking against the assault. The blade cracked the seam open with a final twist, the band fracturing in half. Sparks exploded across the hallway. Gabriel threw the knife aside and ripped at the cuff, pulling the sharp internal teeth free from ruined flesh — no wonder it wouldn’t rotate — and flinching as some kind of off colored fluid sprayed randomly from the damaged mechanism to mix with the blood that was spreading across the floor. Gabriel threw it away from himself and down the corridor without thinking. The voltage that arced through the metal as it left his hand reached back like a last insult and ran up his arm and into his teeth, sending him flinching into himself with a sharp snap that numbed his entire spine and smeared the lights behind his eyes. The hallway took a deep breath when the screaming stopped, and for a moment, no one moved. Nea’s arms were shaking. She pushed herself backward, staring at Wesker’s still form as if expecting him to leap up and resume rearranging their limbs any second. “Is he... Did we just...” Dwight rolled off the pinned shoulder and got to his feet on the second try, scooping Nea up by the elbow. “Come on. We gotta go.” She allowed herself to be hauled swiftly away, reluctantly glancing back one more time at the violence that was spread out across the hall before vanishing around the corner. Jake didn’t move at first, chest rising too fast, eyes flicking between Wesker and the wrecked band on the floor. Then he swore under his breath, grabbed Gabriel by the back of his shirt, and pulled him out of the potential swing radius. After all that, he wasn’t about to risk the killer regaining his senses and decided to take revenge. “You with me?” Jake’s voice pitched low, urgency bleeding through as he tapped Gabriel’s face lightly, trying to get his eyes to focus. “Good. I’m good. Just — numb.” Gabriel coughed. “Go. Go — I’m right behind you.” Jake squeezed his collar once and let go. “Catch up or I’m coming back for you.” “Go. Make sure they get out. I’m alright. Just need a minute.” Jake gave a short nod and jogged off after the others. The corridor was suddenly very large and very empty. The piece of metal lying 20 feet away from Wesker’s hand was still leaking tiny, spitting complaints into the air. The man himself hadn’t moved since the cuff came free. He was bleeding against the cement, the harsh smell of iron and something sour filled the space, and Gabriel couldn’t tell in the moment if he had even survived. Blinking away the shock haze, he rolled to his knees and hauled himself closer. He wasn’t sure why he was keeping his voice down — habit, maybe. Something in him didn’t want to wake anything else. He touched two fingers to Wesker’s neck and waited past the first nothing. The skin was hot and damp and smelled wrong. For a few tense moments, he couldn’t find a pulse. What even happened to killers if they died? Did they have a place they were rebuilt to the way the survivors did? Gabriel frowned and shifted his hand slightly, and there it was: a small, stubborn movement against his fingertips, a flutter that wasn’t rhythm but could be again if given time. He let out a breath he hadn’t noticed holding. He turned Wesker’s wrist gently with his free hand and watched, fascinated and horrified, as the torn edges of skin twitched and tried to think about knitting. It wasn’t a miracle. It wasn’t fast. It was work performed by something that had been denied work for weeks. Thin strands of damaged pulp reached out for others, slowly trying to staunch bleeding and rebuild muscle. On reflex, or possibly some buried compassion, Gabriel pulled an old bandana out of his back pocket and wound it tightly around the gore. At least he wasn’t going to bleed out on the floor after everything. The rest... well that was out of Gabriel’s hands now. Time would tell if it was all worth it, or if they had just repaired their own execution. He got up slowly on unsteady legs, hissing lightly as waking nerves protested the movement. The broken cuff still sparked gently against the floor, whatever fluid it had been spraying now collecting in a puddle around the shards. He put his heel on it and drove his weight down until the housing buckled and the last of the teeth bent in on themselves for good measure, scattering what remained with the side of his shoe. Gabriel leaned against the wall with one hand and worked his way to join up with the rest of the survivors. The Fog coiled around Wesker, waiting for them to leave so it could take what was left of him home. Chapter 15 – Recalibration The Fog didn’t release him — it dropped him. Discarded back to the station, barely short of tumbling down the front steps. Cold tile rushed up to meet him, the impact punching air out of abused lungs and pain into every inch of his body. His spine arched, air rasping in through clenched teeth. Every nerve screamed at once, awareness wrenched cruelly back from the void. Everything either burned or didn’t register at all. His body couldn’t decide which. The world existed in fragments: the buzz of failing lights, the taste of metal in his teeth, a flash of white restraint and hands digging into limbs he could barely control. Muscle tremors chased each other down his arms. His wrist— God, his wrist. It throbbed like a second heart. Still bleeding. Still raw. But when he tried to flex the fingers of that hand, they moved. Sluggishly. Imperfectly. He opened his eyes, squinting against the sterile overhead lighting. It buzzed like a swarm of hornets, fluorescent and cold, washing his vision in pale flicker. Movement tugged at his peripheral. Something dark and crumpled near his arm. He forced his head to turn and found a dark scrap of cloth tied around the wrist — blood-black, soaked through, improvised. Tight. Too tight. For one sharp, irrational second, panic surged — restraint, tightness, pressure around the injury— —but as he grabbed at it to pull it away, his fingers sunk into softness where there was once solid resistance. There was skin beneath the cloth. Not metal. No embedded teeth biting into bone. No hum crawling under the nerves. The cuff was gone. His breath hitched. He stared at the soaked bandana like it might vanish if he blinked. He didn’t know how long he stayed there — only that the thought of moving felt like digging through tar. Somewhere, logic tried to wake up: the survivors, the fight, the knife — hands, entirely too many hands, holding him down while something gave way. They helped him. Why? His thoughts slipped sideways again, fragments scattering before he could catch them, too many systems failing to stay upright at once. He let himself fall with them. The tile was cool. Unmoving. Safe enough. Maybe he’d feel less like scorched earth tomorrow. He closed his eyes as exhaustion sept back in, his body sinking under its own weight. For the first time in weeks, the silence didn’t hurt. As he let rest take his mind from the pain, something stirred gently beneath the skin — faint, sluggish, but there. A pulse. A twitch of black beneath the veins. Uroboros. Healing slower than it ever had, but healing all the same. The footage looped. Frame by frame: a blur of limbs, a flash of steel, the cuff’s detonation flaring across the screen with enough discharged energy to reduce the footage to static for a time. Then the aftermath — Wesker down, the survivors scattering like startled birds. On the desk, the cuff’s remains laid in a mangled heap: metal blackened, circuits cracked, the faint stink of burnt insulation still clinging to it. Useless now. Months of sample collecting. Calibration. Research. Resources spent and prototypes lost. Countless trials. All of it — undone. Ruined by four bleeding nobodies with just enough luck to get in his way. Wesker would be out of commission for days, minimum. And he would never be that easy to corner again. That experiment, for all intents and purposes, was over. Herman closed the connection to the RPD feed with an annoyed huff. There was no reason to watch his failed toy twitch on the ground. He leaned back in the office chair, watching the playback one last time, replaying the moment it all began to fail. The survivors closing in. The pile-on. The knife. The break. He dragged his eyes from the video to the telemetry panel. The cuff’s data stream in the final seconds: readouts spiked red across every channel — neural lock, cardiac suppression, total motor collapse. An overload so complete it nearly killed a demigod. For a heartbeat, even the Entity’s signal drops. Herman exhaled a laugh. “Magnificent.” His eyes flicked back to the footage just in time to catch the cuff’s final arc — when the discharged current jumped to the survivor who removed it, the recoil throwing him back. Herman pauses the frame. Studies it. Conductive discharge. Precision voltage. Adaptive response. Interesting. Yes... there’s something there. Herman's gaze lowered to his own arms, tracing the familiar lines of embedded wire diving in and out of the skin. If he could replicate that — fine-tune it, refine it — If he could isolate that charge — not random, not chaotic — but directed, refined— His mori could become something more. Not just efficient. Not merely brutal. Art. He straightens slowly, pulling up the telemetry logs, eyes hungry as he scrolls. The cuff was made for one body. Too specific. Too delicate. The average human body is messier. Variable. It would need to be consistent. Measured. Flexible within a narrow range. Calibrated to multiple subjects. A proper formula. A real challenge to get just right. Which meant he would need test subjects. A pity about Wesker — but failures only prove the system works, even if for a time. Fortunately, survivors were much easier to collect than killers. And it had been so very long since he had truly challenged himself. The Entity hadn’t stopped him before. And that, at least to him, was permission enough. He closed the failed file marked 06-W. Opened a new one. EXPERIMENT 07 – Electrophysiological Adaptation Trials. His pen scratched across the page. A note. A hum. A smile that didn’t reach his eyes. The lights flickered — patient, waiting. “Let’s begin again.”
